policyFindings: Broadened ordinary base adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, numerals, pronouns and independently lexicalized interjections are linguistically reasonable; noun/adj/infinitive-only would add an unsupported exclusion.
Inspect raw_tags and gloss text in addition to normalized tags: ANDE has raw subestándar; AMOS/GOLES explicitly state obsolete/rare in gloss but lack matching normalized tags.
Plural-only noun meanings can be bare lemma entries lacking plural tags: combine source text/usage with morphology, preserving invariant singulars and standalone interjections.

A feminine singular common noun can be an ordinary eligible lexical item even if extractor calls it form-of; do not rescue it using a different obscure noun sense. Base-adjective agreement forms remain distinct.

Spelling-level Zipf cannot establish eligible-sense frequency, especially for common verb forms, personal names and place names. Commonness exclusions in this review are model linguistic judgments, not measured sense-frequency statistics.

The prototype allows obsolete/archaic/rare alternative senses whenever another sense qualifies. Eligibility should use a qualifying ordinary sense, and teaching should select that sense rather than the first surviving rare/technical entry.
Labels such as botanical range or musical origin in a gloss do not by themselves prove a word is exclusively used in that region. Do not impose geographic-name based word bans.

No blanket prohibition on words having vulgar secondary senses: NEGRO and ordinary benign nouns must survive. Separately review words whose ordinary Mexican reading is offensive while surviving benign senses are specialized.
